items.feedback: That's right, because an agent is defined by its structure: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result returns for the next step. A longer prompt or bigger model only changes one call.

That's right, because the model only outputs a structured request naming check_calendar and its arguments. The program around it runs the tool and sends the result back, so the model never touches the booking system.

No, an agent repeating the same failing edit gets no new information, so more time will not fix it. That belief is M6: a loop needs a stopping condition, such as a step limit that ends it and reports back.

Your count of 4 is right: three tool requests plus the final answer. But the model does not run any tool; it only requests one, and the program runs it. Your wording shows M4, the model runs tools itself.

That's right, because the program feeds the result back as the model's next input and calls it again, so the model can use it to choose its next step. The group-chat reply analogy fits that loop well.

Not quite: the name helps, but the model reads the whole description the program gives it, meaning the name, what the tool does and its parameters. A vague name like run_task would mislead without that text.

summary: You have the loop down: what makes an agent, what the model outputs for a tool call, and where results go. Fix two things: the program runs every tool and the model only requests it (M4), and a loop needs a stopping condition (M6). Next, redo q3 and q6, then write a one-line description for check_calendar.
